This came out of the prompt below. Read what it says about itself: project locations are derived from public reporting and are labeled with their precision — none are surveyed parcel boundaries. That sentence is the judgment part, and it's the difference between a map you can use and one you can't.

The exercise — try it yourself

  1. Here's the page I made, and here's the prompt I used to make it.
  2. Open whatever AI you have — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot. Use a different one than the person next to you.
  3. Run the same prompt. Or change it, if you want something else.
  4. Look at what came back. Compare with each other — what did each one give you?
  5. What's actually right? What would you have to check before you'd show it to anybody?
The prompt — copy this whole block 
Build me a single self-contained HTML file that shows an interactive map of the Paluxy River watershed in north-central Texas.

Include these layers:

* The watershed boundary. It's HUC-10 code `1206020201`. Pull it live from the USGS Watershed Boundary Dataset at `https://hydro.nationalmap.gov/arcgis/rest/services/wbd/MapServer`, layer 5, using `f=geojson`. Zoom the map to fit it.
* Rivers and streams, from the USGS National Hydrography Dataset at `https://hydro.nationalmap.gov/arcgis/rest/services/nhd/MapServer`.
* Land cover, as a WMS layer from `https://www.mrlc.gov/geoserver/mrlc_display/wms`, layer name `mrlc_display:NLCD_2021_Land_Cover_L48`. Give me a slider to change how transparent it is, and a legend that names what each color means.
* A basemap I can switch between topographic and aerial imagery.
* Checkboxes to turn each layer on and off.

Use Leaflet 1.9.4 from a CDN. Put all the HTML, CSS and JavaScript in one file so I can open it by double-clicking it. If a layer fails to load, show me a message telling me which one, instead of just failing quietly.
  • github.com/rivuletsteph/paluxy_watershedThe repo for this map — currently private

How I keep track of all of it

The map ahead — from here to the end of the yearbe•do
Work lanes only. Eleven projects running in one of them, and this class talk is one bar on it.
The wheel at the end of a daybe•do
Eight areas — earth, body, water, heart, air, mind, fire, spirit. What got attention that day, and what didn't.
  • Several projects at once — I'd lose most of it holding it in my head
  • Overwhelm is the real obstacle, more than any missing skill
  • Externalizing my thinking is most of what this does. It's been an expansive thing for me, not a tidy-up

What's actually in it — four layers

  • Rhythms — which lane of my life something belongs to. Nine of them, named by me
  • Drives — run months, carry a target. My defined role inside a project
  • Destinations — run years, never carry a target. The test is whether you can arrive
  • Guides — the stars I steer by. Never scored, never dated, never closed
  • Plus eight wellness areas that read what a moment is about — earth, body, water, heart, air, mind, fire, spirit. I never pick those; the system reads them

Why I bother

  • It catches the small things — the tier below what memory holds on its own
  • It surfaces the next right thing rather than nagging me with everything
  • Being intentional about the route: you can push uphill every day, or wind around the mountain and save your energy for the fight that actually needs fighting
  • People fight fires because they think they have no choice. We always have a choice — that's a lot of what this system is about
Pain is mandatory. Suffering is optional.

Being a context architect

  • Most AI failures now are context failures, not capability ones
  • You can't use context you never wrote down
  • AI amplifies what you give it — and context is what you give it
You could start this today

Open any AI and tell it what you did today, in whatever order it comes out. Ask it to sort what matters from what doesn't. That's the whole beginning — mine started there and it's still in development.

The long path

The one question to carry out of here

Does this expand my capabilities, or diminish them?

Tiago Forte, Forte Labs. Ask it every time you reach for it.

Why you might be anxious — it isn't just a feeling

89%
of grads worry AI could replace entry-level roles — up from 64% a year earlier
36%
feel their college prepared them to use AI at work
82% vs 41%
grads who worked during college landed entry-level jobs at double the rate

Figures gathered Aug 2026 from Forbes, Monster, CNBC and NACE reporting. Spot-check before this goes public.

  • The jobs most exposed are the ones new grads compete for — data entry, basic coding, admin, customer service. The prove-yourself-on-the-easy-stuff rung
  • That last number is the one I'd act on. Get real experience while you're still in school

The intertidal

  • Longpath's word for it: a period where the old ways of being no longer work and the new ones are still emerging
  • That's a real thing to be standing in. It isn't only loss — it's also unusual leverage

What her students say

Even Stanford students reflect some of this mixed sentiment. There is anxiety. There is sense of hope. There is also excitement. There is also confusion. There's also simultaneously a sense of dignity and agency when AI can help me do things that I couldn't do before — and a sense of loss of dignity and agency if AI is going to take my job. Fei-Fei Li — The Godmother of AI Reveals What Comes Next, Moconomy · 16:27
Students who are not properly motivated can use technology as a lazy crutch instead of an empowering learning tool. I worry about that a lot. Fei-Fei Li — 20:12

Taking a long path approach

  • I try to take a long path approach to my own life and my own work — that's what the map at the start was
  • My path didn't start with me and it won't end with me. I have a kid
  • Same move at a larger scale: decisions made this year set the water table for people not born yet
  • Longpath Megatrends — the forces worth planning against: demographic · social and cultural · science and technology · economic · environmental · political
  • Longpath — Ari WallachDecisions made with several generations in view
The arc of history is long. I paraphrase Dr. King. I believe it bends towards benevolence… we have it in our DNA, we want our offspring to live a better life. Fei-Fei Li — 22:24

Build both halves

AI produces the map. It doesn't decide what map is worth making.

And it doesn't stand in a room with a skeptical landowner and explain why it matters.

  • Careful here: GIS itself is not the automation-resistant part. Digitizing, spatial joins, watershed delineation, writing the ArcPy — that's exactly where the tools are moving fastest. If all you have is "I can make a map in ArcGIS," that's more exposed than it feels
  • What holds: physical presence · judgment under ambiguity · interpersonal trust
  • Being there · knowing when a number looks wrong · sitting down with a landowner
  • Get the field reps while you can
  • Transgenerational empathy — Longpath again. In a watershed that isn't abstract: what you decide about it today runs forward for decades
  • Texas Stream TeamVolunteer water quality monitoring — they need people
